paragraphs.source_en: Given that the latter room always shared a back wall with a house on the next street, the back rooms probably had no windows. These structures are closer to the scale of cells than houses, much too small for a family, and yet they seem to have been lived in.20 Nothing like these houses is known from elsewhere in Mesopotamia—​not only are they so small and regular, they do not even have burials under their floors.21 naditums and Scribal Students 295 All this makes sense if they were gagum homes. A single naditum, living alone, might have found such a small house perhaps cramped, but not unlivable. The neighborhood would have been full of women, all of them devoted to the sun god.

paragraphs.source_en: We know that many of the naditums also owned houses in Sippar in other neighborhoods outside the gagum; perhaps they didn’t live in their gagum rooms all the time and often enjoyed the more spacious quarters of their second homes. The naditums were buried in a cemetery, which also explains the lack of burials under the houses.

paragraphs.source_en: About fourteen tablets from the excavations in the 1980s clearly seem to have come from this neighborhood of tiny houses.22 Eight of them pertained to the activities of women, including three letters apparently written by or to women,23 a silver payment by a woman,24 a loan payment by a woman,25 two loans taken by women,26 and a note recording dates delivered to a woman.27 The contracts among these documents were witnessed almost entirely by women, and many of the female names were the ones typical of naditums.
